Jehoshaphat
jeh-HOSH-a-fat
proper noun (figure)
Hebrew Yehoshaphat (H3092) — "Yahweh judges" or "Yahweh has judged." From Yah (the divine name) + shaphat ("to judge, to vindicate").

📖 Biblical Definition

Jehoshaphat (c. 873 — 849 BC) was the fourth king of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (1 Kings 22:41-50; 2 Chronicles 17-20), son of the reforming king Asa, who reigned twenty-five years and is presented in the canonical record as one of the half-dozen most faithful kings of the Judahite line. His name — "Yahweh judges" — was vindicated in his program of reform: he removed the high places (partly — the record is candid that some remained, 2 Chr 20:33), sent Levites throughout Judah with the book of the law to teach the people (2 Chr 17:7-9 — the first king-led national catechesis in the history of Judah), strengthened the cities and fortified the kingdom, and established a judicial reform in Jerusalem (2 Chr 19:5-11) that anchored the courts in Yahweh's character: "Take heed what ye do: for ye judge not for man, but for the LORD, who is with you in the judgment." His great failure was political-marital: he married his son Jehoram to Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel of Israel, an alliance that would nearly destroy the Davidic dynasty within a generation (the Athaliah usurpation, 2 Kings 11). His military narrative includes two great episodes: at Ramoth-Gilead with Ahab (the disastrous joint campaign in which Ahab disguised himself and was killed anyway by an "arrow at a venture," 1 Kings 22), and the Valley of Beracah deliverance (2 Chr 20), where a vast Moabite-Ammonite-Mehunite coalition was destroyed by the LORD himself without Judah lifting a sword — Jehoshaphat's prayer in that chapter ("O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee") is one of the great Old Testament prayers of weakness and faith. The book of Joel later prophesies of the "Valley of Jehoshaphat" (Joel 3:2, 12) as the place of God's final judgment of the nations — eschatological vocabulary built on his name.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Fourth king of Judah (c. 873-849 BC); son of the reforming Asa; reigned 25 years; instituted national catechesis by sending Levites with the book of the law (2 Chr 17); delivered miraculously at the Valley of Beracah (2 Chr 20); name means 'Yahweh judges'.

JEHOSHAPHAT, proper noun. Hebrew Yehoshaphat (H3092) — "Yahweh judges" or "Yahweh has judged."

Fourth king of Judah (c. 873-849 BC); son of Asa; reigned 25 years.

Major reform king: removed high places (partially); sent Levites with the book of the law throughout Judah for national catechesis (2 Chr 17:7-9); established judicial reform in Jerusalem (2 Chr 19:5-11).

Famous deliverances: Ramoth-Gilead campaign with Ahab (1 Kings 22), Valley of Beracah miracle (2 Chr 20).

His name lent to the eschatological "Valley of Jehoshaphat" of Joel 3:2, 12.

📖 Key Scripture

2 Chronicles 17:7-9 — "Also in the third year of his reign he sent to his princes... and with them he sent Levites... And they taught in Judah, and had the book of the law of the LORD with them, and went about throughout all the cities of Judah, and taught the people."

2 Chronicles 19:6-7 — "And [Jehoshaphat] said to the judges, Take heed what ye do: for ye judge not for man, but for the LORD, who is with you in the judgment. Wherefore now let the fear of the LORD be upon you; take heed and do it: for there is no iniquity with the LORD our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of gifts."

2 Chronicles 20:12 — "O our God, wilt thou not judge them? for we have no might against this great company that cometh against us; neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee."

Joel 3:12 — "Let the heathen be wakened, and come up to the valley of Jehoshaphat: for there will I sit to judge all the heathen round about."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Jehoshaphat is corrupted when his Beracah deliverance is treated as merely a battle-victory rather than as a paradigm of corporate prayer and trust, when his judicial reform is overlooked beside his more dramatic narratives, or when his disastrous marriage-alliance with Ahab is excused on political grounds rather than read as the doctrinal warning Scripture intends.

expand to see more

Beracah as battle-tactics. The Valley of Beracah deliverance (2 Chr 20) has sometimes been treated as a one-off military miracle — the LORD ambushing the enemy coalition while Judah sang. The chapter itself is constructed as a paradigm: corporate fasting, public prayer of weakness, prophetic word through Jahaziel, worship-as-warfare (Levites singing before the army), trust without sword. The chapter teaches how a Christian people approaches overwhelming adversity, not just how Judah won one battle. Read for the paradigm; do not stop at the tactics.

Ahab-alliance excused as politics. Jehoshaphat married his son Jehoram to Athaliah, Ahab and Jezebel's daughter, almost certainly as a politically calculated north-south alliance to stabilize the divided kingdom against Aramean and Assyrian pressure. The Chronicler refuses the political defense: "shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD?" (2 Chr 19:2). The alliance directly produced the Athaliah usurpation (2 Kings 11) and nearly extinguished the Davidic line. The doctrinal lesson is exactly what the Chronicler intended: unequal-yoke alliances with covenant-rejecting partners eventually destroy what they were meant to preserve.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yehoshaphat (H3092) — "Yahweh judges," from Yah (divine name) + shaphat ("to judge"). The fourth king of Judah; his name lent to the eschatological Valley of Jehoshaphat (Joel 3).

Hebrew Yehoshaphat (H3092) — "Yahweh judges" or "Yahweh has judged"

Compound: Yah (the divine name) + shaphat ("to judge, to vindicate, to govern")

Fourth king of the divided southern kingdom of Judah (c. 873-849 BC); son of Asa

Major reform king; introduced national Levitical catechesis (2 Chr 17:7-9); established judicial reform (2 Chr 19)

His name lent to Joel 3:2, 12 "Valley of Jehoshaphat" — the eschatological place of God's judgment of the nations

"Jehoshaphat — the reforming king of Judah whose name means 'Yahweh judges'."

"Our eyes are upon thee — the Beracah prayer that has become a paradigm of Christian weakness-and-faith."
